papers.title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
papers.abstract: Cardiac autonomic activity is observed only through beat-to-beat (RR) intervals, and separating it into parasympathetic-like and sympathetic-like components is an inverse problem that RR alone is not expected to solve uniquely. We introduce SPARK (Stochastic Phase-domain Autonomic Reconstruction Kinetics), a state-space model in which two independent, mean-reverting latent drives modulate heart rate through an integrate-and-fire pacemaker. The model is combined with exact continuous-time Kalman filtering and with an explicit physiological identification structure: time-scale priors, a kinetic ordering and a spectral partition of heart rate variability. SPARK offers a model-conditional description of autonomic trajectories that complements conventional heart rate variability; its latent states are reconstructions, not measurements of neural activity. Across recordings, fitting each recording from many different starting points gave a median of 23.5 distinct solutions without physiological information versus 1.0 with it, and one process absorbed essentially all the variability in 75% versus 4% of the fits; the fit diagnostics showed residual structure in most recordings. Reconstructions were then examined: in 10 tilt-table recordings, the vagal-like state decreased and the sympathetic-like state increased in 10 of 10; exploratory comparisons between 20 young and 20 older adults showed differences in reconstructed variability and faster-component kinetics, although several latent summaries were mathematically redundant; and in 263 exercise recordings, median recovery times, which are closely tied to the fitted time constants, were 42 s (vagal-like) and 341 s (sympathetic-like). How a stressor-induced change is split between the two drives remained sensitive to the spectral anchor.

papers.title: Skeletal muscle aging drives sex- and compartment-specific protein insolubility that is modifiable by proteostasis-directed treatments
papers.abstract: Protein aggregation and altered protein solubility indicate proteostatic decline, yet their roles in skeletal muscle aging remain poorly understood. We combined light and electron microscopy, quantitative proteomics, and stable-isotope labeling of skeletal muscle to investigate age-associated changes in protein insolubility, and their responses to exercise and rapamycin. Aged muscle accumulated distinct aggresome and amyloid-positive aggregates despite unchanged bulk insoluble protein content. Instead, aging altered the abundance and soluble-insoluble shifts of lower-abundance proteins across cellular components, particularly mitochondrial, nuclear and extracellular matrix proteins, with greater changes in females. These changes were not broadly explained by intrinsic protein aggregation propensity. Exercise and rapamycin partially reversed age-associated changes in abundance and partitioning without increasing protein synthesis. Together, these findings highlight sex- and cellular component-dependent changes in protein insolubility as important, modifiable aspects of skeletal muscle proteostasis, and indicate that proteostatic maintenance may be a more important target than anabolism for muscle aging.

papers.title: Analysis of haemolysis-based injury in immortalised proximal tubule epithelial cells is impaired by haemoglobin interference with bioluminescence assays.
papers.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a serious complication which is common amongst cardiac and aortic/vascular surgery patients. Although the cause of AKI following cardiac surgery is multifactorial, haemolysis is an increasingly recognised contributing factor caused by the use of cardiopulmonary bypass machines. Haemolysis, the lysis of red blood cells, releases free haemoglobin (fHb) into the bloodstream which is known to cause kidney injury. Currently, the mechanisms of haemolysis-induced kidney injury are not fully understood. In this study, we investigated the injury response to fHb in a human-derived conditionally immortalised proximal tubule epithelial cell line (ciPTECs). Results showed that fHb interference reduces bioluminescence signal output which is considerably mitigated by removing fHb solutions and haemolysed plasma prior to the beginning of the assay. Interestingly, we found that the effect of fHb on ciPTECs was different with haemolysed plasma compared to fHb solutions, potentially due to factors other than fHb within the plasma. In contrast to expectations, haemolysed plasma induced only a marginal increase in NF-B activity and had minimal effect on mitochondrial function. Together, these findings suggest that caution should be applied when using bioluminescent assays with fHb, both in solution and haemolysed plasma, and that fHb may not inflict severe injury on ciPTECs.

papers.title: Enhanced hypoxic ventilatory response is accompanied by a decrease in carotid body mitochondrial oxygen affinity in heart failure
papers.abstract: Carotid bodies (CBs), the main peripheral oxygen sensors, play a significant role in sympathetic overdrive in heart failure (HF), resulting in worse clinical outcomes. Whilst CBs are an attractive therapeutic target, the development of CB focused therapies has been limited as the oxygen sensing mechanism is not fully understood. It has been hypothesised that the oxygen sensor is part of mitochondrial complex IV, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) signalling plays a crucial role in the oxygen sensing cascade. However, changes to CB mitochondrial function have never been determined in HF. Hence, we aimed to address this gap by characterising CB mitochondrial function and ROS production using a rapid pacing ovine model of HF. The hypoxic ventilatory response (HVR) and autonomic function were assessed pre- and post HF induction. Tissue homogenates were prepared from whole CBs from control and HF and utilised to measure kinetics of mitochondrial oxygen affinity, respiration and H2O2 production rates by high-resolution respirometry. In HF, HVR and sympathetic drive were increased, while complex IV oxygen affinity was decreased. Despite an increase in abundance of mitochondrial complexes, no changes in mitochondrial respiration or H2O2 production were observed. However, aconitase activity and lipid peroxidation level were increased in HF. Overall, these results suggest that the CB mitochondrial function is altered in HF, and decreased CB mitochondrial oxygen affinity may suggest a higher complex IV oxygen sensitivity. Higher oxygen sensitivity accompanied by an increased oxidative stress may be key drivers of CB overactivity and therefore autonomic imbalance in HF.

papers.title: Trunk muscle activity across various trunk-limb coordination patterns in centipede locomotion
papers.abstract: Animals coordinate movements of their limbs and flexible bodies, yet how trunk muscle activity changes across locomotor patterns remains unclear. We simultaneously recorded electromyograms from trunk muscles (deep dorsal oblique muscles) and trunk-limb kinematics in two centipede species exhibiting retrograde and direct locomotor waves during swimming and walking. During swimming, trunk muscle activity followed a similar phase relationship with trunk bending in both species despite opposite wave directions and different involvement of limbs, suggesting common active generation of undulation. During fast walking, trunk muscle activity was strongest around the ipsilateral swing phase in the undulatory retrograde-wave gait of Scolopendra mutilans, but weaker and associated with the ipsilateral stance phase despite the nearly straight trunk in the direct-wave gait of Scolopocryptops rubiginosus. Together, our findings suggest that the same trunk muscles serve two contrasting mechanical roles depending on locomotor mode: either generating trunk undulation or actively straightening the trunk against limb-induced deformation.

papers.title: Quantifying and Visualizing the Invisible Hazard of Infant Rebreathing
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Rebreathing of expired gases during prone infant sleeping contributes to hypoxic and hypercapnic exposure, even without airway obstruction. We investigated how anatomical, physiological, and environmental factors influence aerodynamic rebreathing. METHODS: A dynamically scaled in vitro model simulated prone nasal breathing corresponding to infants weighing 2 to 5 kg, with nostril diameters of 3.2 to 6.0 mm and breathing frequencies of 25 to 40 breaths/min. Ambient temperature and sleep-surface characteristics were varied. Rebreathing was quantified using tracer measurements, while flow visualization revealed the underlying aerodynamic mechanisms. RESULTS: Rebreathing exceeded 60% despite unobstructed nasal openings. Increasing ambient temperature from 23 to 30 degrees C increased rebreathing by 68 to 77%, while reducing simulated infant mass from 5 to 2 kg increased rebreathing by 39 to 46%. Fibrous surfaces increased rebreathing, particularly near inclined nasal openings. A novel finding was that increasing nostril diameter from 3.2 to 6.0 mm increased rebreathing by up to 50%. Flow visualization revealed vortical structures that retained expired fluid near the nasal openings, facilitating re-inspiration. CONCLUSIONS: Aerodynamic rebreathing depends strongly on simulated infant characteristics and sleeping environments. These findings are consistent with established safe-sleep recommendations and identify nostril diameter, for the first time, as a potentially important anatomical factor warranting clinical investigation.

papers.title: Ribosomal Remodeling and Translational Suppression in the Post-Arrest Heart
papers.abstract: Background: Cardiac arrest (CA) is a leading cause of death and disability in the United States, and no pharmacologic therapies improve post-arrest outcomes. Acute myocardial dysfunction is a highly prevalent CA complication that contributes to post-arrest mortality, yet the molecular mechanisms that drive this dysfunction remain incompletely understood. Prior work in our laboratory has suggested that ribosome-associated pathways are altered after CA in the heart and that translational dysregulation may be a central feature of post-arrest myocardial injury. Objectives: To define the impact of CA on myocardial ribosome biology and protein synthesis across experimental models of CA and determine how transcriptome, ribosome-bound transcriptome, translational efficiency, and proteome changes evolve after CA in the heart. Methods: We studied complementary porcine and murine models of CA. In pigs, left ventricular myocardium was collected from naive controls, cardiac arrest with return of spontaneous circulation (Arrest), and cardiac arrest with pulseless electrical activity (PEA) re-arrest in a myocardial infarction-induced CA model and analyzed tissue by RNA sequencing. In mice, left ventricular tissue was collected at various time points after potassium chloride-induced asystole and resuscitation for ribosome activity and multi-omic profiling including RNA sequencing, ribosome profiling, and proteomics. Results: In the porcine model, myocardial transcriptomes demonstrate enrichment of cytosolic ribosomal protein transcripts and translation-related pathways that increase with ischemic burden. In contrast, a functional assay of ribosome activity in mice demonstrates suppression of protein synthesis after CA with gradual recovery over days. Multi-omic profiling in the mouse model demonstrates that ribosome- and translation-related pathways are among the most consistently altered programs across time points and modalities. While 6 h studies note prevalent inflammatory signals, 24 h studies find disruptions to ion homeostasis and conduction-related pathways that are likely related to translational suppression. Conclusions: CA induces marked remodeling of myocardial ribosome biology, characterized by increasing ribosomal transcripts with ischemic burden in the pig model. However, functional studies in the mouse model demonstrate that ribosome activity is suppressed following CA and remains suppressed for at least 24 h after resuscitation, contributing to reduced nascent protein synthesis and may limit critical functions of the heart. These findings identify translational control as a central feature of post-arrest myocardial injury and suggest that ribosome-dependent recovery pathways may represent a novel therapeutic target in post-arrest cardiac dysfunction.

papers.title: Isocaloric restriction of a high-fat diet under TAK-242 administration: metabolic and gut microbial responses in mice
papers.abstract: High-fat feeding promotes obesity in mice largely by increasing energy intake, so diet composition and energy intake are hard to separate without pair-feeding. We previously showed that isocaloric restriction normalizes body weight, glycemia and plasma lipids but not visceral adiposity, adipose inflammation or the fecal microbial community. We hypothesized that, during administration of the TLR4 signaling inhibitor TAK-242, matching energy intake to that of low-fat controls would normalize adiposity, intestinal barrier gene expression and the fecal microbial community. Male C57BL/6 mice (n = 8 per group) received a low-fat diet, a high-fat diet ad libitum, or a high-fat diet pair-fed to controls from week 0 or week 5 for 12 weeks; TAK-242 (3 ug/g, three times weekly) was given to every group from week 0.4, with no vehicle-injected arm. Intake did not differ among groups during a three-week low-fat acclimation (P = .88); over the 12 weeks on the assigned diets the ad libitum high-fat group ate 5.5% more than controls (P = .50). Over the full trajectory the ad libitum high-fat group gained 0.48 g/week more than controls (group x week, P = .012); both pair-fed groups had lower fasting glucose than that group. Adipocyte diameter, visceral fat proportion, ileal barrier genes, CCK-induced satiation and microbial alpha diversity did not differ significantly among groups. Adipose Ccl2 expression differed (P = .043, exploratory), as did fecal community composition (PERMANOVA P = .022), although no pairwise contrast survived correction. Energy restriction did not return the microbial community toward the low-fat profile.

papers.title: Epigenetic Rescue of Disuse Muscle Atrophy by Histone Deacetylase Inhibitor Trichostatin A
papers.abstract: Mechanical unloading rapidly induces skeletal muscle atrophy and functional deterioration, yet how the loss of mechanical input influences nuclear architecture, chromatin organization, and associated transcriptional programs remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated whether pharmacological inhibition of histone deacetylases (HDACs) using Trichostatin A (TSA) could attenuate the consequences of continued mechanical unloading in a murine hindlimb suspension model. Following 14 days of unloading, mice exhibited impaired locomotor activity, altered muscle architecture, and widespread transcriptional reprogramming characterized by increased expression of atrophy associated genes, inflammatory mediators, and extracellular matrix remodeling pathways, alongside suppression of mitochondrial metabolic programs. Super resolution imaging further revealed irregular Lamin A/C organization and disruption of discrete H3K9me3 associated heterochromatin foci. Systemic TSA treatment significantly attenuated the decline in locomotor activity, accompanied by trends toward reduced body weight loss, and preservation of muscle morphology. Transcriptomic analysis demonstrated a substantial shift toward the baseline expression profile, with high-dose TSA attenuating FOXO associated catabolic programs, inflammatory, and extracellular matrix-related signatures, while enhancing mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation pathways. Quantitative gene level and pathway analyses further revealed dose dependent and selective reversal of unloading associated transcriptional changes. Notably, TSA treatment also partially preserved nuclear lamina organization and the focal distribution of H3K9me3 associated heterochromatin. Despite these muscle specific benefits, TSA did not prevent trabecular bone loss over the 14-day unloading period, although several muscle-expressed genes potentially involved in muscle to bone communication were altered by treatment. Together, these findings demonstrate that HDAC inhibition counteracts multiple functional and molecular consequences of skeletal muscle unloading and is associated with partial preservation of nuclear and heterochromatin organization. This study supports a link between mechanical unloading, nuclear architectural remodeling, and HDAC sensitive transcriptional regulation, providing a foundation for epigenetic strategies to counter disuse induced muscle deterioration.

papers.title: Responses of Muscle Volume, Strength, and Motor Unit Properties to Bed Rest and Retraining in Young Males and Females
papers.abstract: Sex differences in motor unit (MU) properties to simulated microgravity are unknown. Young males and females completed a 21-day head-down bed rest followed by a 21-day retraining. Bed rest reduced knee extensor strength and volume without sex differences. MU firing rate decreased in both groups, more in females, alongside increased serum C-terminal agrin fragment. After retraining, these measures returned to baseline, whereas strength only partially recovered, remaining below baseline.

papers.title: Satellite cell glucocorticoid receptor restrains myogenic commitment without mediating the effects of therapeutic glucocorticoids on muscle repair
papers.abstract: Glucocorticoids (GCs) exert profound effects on skeletal muscle, but the contribution of satellite cell (SatC) glucocorticoid receptor (GR) signaling to muscle regeneration remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the role of GR in SatC homeostasis and assessed whether SatC GR mediates the effects of therapeutic GCs on muscle repair. Conditional deletion of GR in SatC reduced the number of PAX7-positive cells during regeneration in young mice, but did not substantially impair muscle repair in either young or aged animals. Transcriptomic and chromatin profiling revealed that GR occupies genes involved in stem cell fate and developmental signaling, with extensive GR binding already established in quiescent SatC. GR-deficient quiescent SatC showed reduced expression of Yap1, Runx1 and Foxo1, together with increased Myog expression. Similarly, GR silencing in human myoblasts induced early myogenic differentiation markers without affecting proliferation, supporting a conserved role for GR in restraining myogenic commitment. We next examined the effects of two therapeutic GCs on muscle regeneration. Chronic prednisone treatment altered the transcriptional landscape of regenerating muscle in an age-dependent manner, without substantially affecting histological repair. In contrast, dexamethasone administration during the early inflammatory phase delayed regeneration, with persistent necrosis and increased collagen deposition. These effects were comparable in control and SatC-specific GR-deficient mice, indicating that they do not require GR in SatC. Together, these findings identify GR as a regulator of the quiescent, undifferentiated state of SatC, while showing that the effects of therapeutic GCs on muscle repair are largely independent of SatC GR. They further highlight the importance of treatment regimen and physiological context in determining the effects of GCs on skeletal muscle regeneration.

papers.title: Residual Hearing Loss After Chronic Cochlear Implantation in Guinea Pigs is Primarily Conductive
papers.abstract: It is desirous to preserve residual low-frequency hearing in cochlear implant recipients, as dual stimulation using electrical and acoustic signals results in superior speech-in-noise processing and musicality. However, cochlear implant recipients commonly lose their residual acoustic hearing gradually following surgical placement of the array. The governing mechanism is not understood and is likely due to multiple factors including surgical trauma, inflammation, and the foreign body induced immune response to the array, including formation of intracochlear fibrosis. Normal mechanical function of the cochlea is expected to underpin residual hearing but has not been directly studied. This function includes efficient transmission of sound to the cochlea via the middle ear, sound propagation via the basilar membrane travelling wave, mechanical tuning characteristics, and the non-linear cochlear amplification of responses to low-frequency stimulation. Here, we examined these features in cochleae and middle ears of unimplanted, acutely and chronically implanted guinea pigs using our minimally invasive preparation and optical coherence tomography vibrometry. We observed that mechanical tuning and amplification is not significantly altered by either acute or chronic implant. However, the response threshold was raised and proportional to middle ear responses. Additionally, the organ of Corti phase, and its sound intensity dependent changes, are unaltered by CI. Finally, a cluster analysis revealed sensitivity loss in chronically implanted animals is caused by middle ear dysfunction. Hence, in the guinea pig model, the dominant etiology of residual hearing loss is conductive. More research is required to establish whether residual hearing loss in humans similarly shares conductive elements.

papers.title: High latitude, high tolerance: Northern juvenile Chinook salmon exhibit substantial thermal plasticity and acute heat tolerance
papers.abstract: In a rapidly warming North, Chinook salmon are facing rising river temperatures, increasing frequencies of heat waves, and greater annual thermal variation. These factors have putatively contributed to substantial declines in Alaska Chinook salmon abundance; understanding the thermal sensitivity and acclimation capacity of Chinook salmon at the northern extents of their range is therefore imperative. To this end, we acclimated juvenile Yukon River Chinook to five ecologically relevant summer temperatures (12.5, 15, 17.5, 20, and 22.5{degrees}C) under two feeding treatments of 100% or 40% satiation. We then assessed whole organism heat tolerance at rest and while swimming, along with the thermal sensitivity of heart rate and cardiac electrical activity. Yukon River Chinook substantially increased whole organism heat tolerance at rest and under exercise with warm acclimation. Cardiac heat tolerance also increased, and fish showed marked thermal compensation of maximum heart rate, resetting it to lower levels with warm acclimation. Feed treatment had a limited effect outside of peak heart rate and the transition temperatures of Q10. Warm acclimation was also associated with a shortening of the PR and QRS intervals and a lengthening of the QT interval. Across all acclimation groups, the PR interval plateaued to an extent far greater than heart rate itself, suggesting that limitations to AV conduction may limit cardiac function at high acute temperatures. Altogether, high latitude juvenile Chinook display remarkable heat tolerance and thermal plasticity, which may be preserved in association with the large seasonal, weather dependent, and spatial thermal variation Yukon River Chinook face during freshwater rearing and along with their extensive seaward and return migrations. The acute heat tolerance of Yukon River Chinook, which is comparable to or outperforming lower latitude Chinook and other salmonids, emphasizes the need for population-specific work for informed conservation efforts.

papers.title: Functional Assessment and Extended Culture of Human Pediatric Cardiac Tissue Slices for Preclinical Testing
papers.abstract: Background: Living human myocardial slices preserve native tissue architecture, but their application to pediatric cardiac physiology or prolonged functional testing remains limited. We adapted a passive culture method for small surgical myocardial specimens obtained from patients with congenital heart disease (CHD). Methods: Atrial and ventricular specimens were obtained from 41 cardiac surgery patients (7.7{+/-}11.1 years; 1 day-49 years). Myocardial tissue was sectioned into slices and studied acutely, or maintained under free floating, rocking cell culture conditions without electrical or mechanical stimulation. Calcium transients were recorded in response to external pacing (0.2-2 Hz) at baseline, and after isoproterenol or norepinephrine exposure. Selected preparations underwent viability, histological, and gene expression analyses. Results: Pacing evoked calcium transients were recorded from all four cardiac chambers, exhibiting expected frequency-dependent shortening. Mean interslice and intraslice coefficients of variation were 11.1% and 7.6%. Viability was 85.8 {+/-} 5.6% post-slicing and 78.8 {+/-} 5.0% after 3-5 hours. Calcium transients remained detectable through 178 days in atrial and 119 days in ventricular slices. Calcium transient durations were relatively stable during extended culture. Beta-adrenergic agonists shortened calcium transient durations (isoproterenol: 32% atrial, 25% ventricular at 0.3 Hz); responses to isoproterenol persisted to approximately 120 days in selected atrial slices and 60 days in ventricular slices. Selected histological features were preserved, although some extracellular matrix and apoptosis related transcripts changed. Conclusions: Small surgical specimens support repeated physiological measurements and pharmacological testing during extended passive culture, providing a platform for human developmental and disease-specific cardiac research.

papers.title: mTORC1-dependent control of Hedgehog signaling mediates nutrient-responsive licensing of intestinal stem cell differentiation
papers.abstract: How progenitor cells couple their metabolic state to the regulation of fate and differentiation remains a fundamental question in tissue development and regeneration. Here, we identify a nutrient-responsive circuit that links progenitor anabolism to differentiation in the Drosophila midgut. We show that the mTORC1 downstream effector PWP1 is necessary and sufficient for differentiation of intestinal stem cell progeny toward the absorptive lineage in fed animals. In progenitors with high mTORC1 activity, PWP1 controls gene expression to promote Hedgehog (Hh) signaling, which cell autonomously drives progenitor differentiation into enterocytes. This circuit is constrained by feedback regulation, as elevated Hh activity inhibits mTORC1 and consequently excludes PWP1 from the nucleus. Disruption of the mTORC1-PWP1-Hh axis causes a progressive failure of enterocyte turnover during aging and reduced lifespan. While the aged midguts retain their barrier function, defective renewal leads to aging-associated deregulation of intestinal metabolism. Collectively, these observations support the concept of growth-dependent licensing of differentiation, whereby the nutrient-responsive anabolic state of a progenitor cell controls its lineage progression, consequently enabling organ renewal.

papers.title: A microstructural analysis of water intake patterns associated with light phase food and water restriction in male and female rats.
papers.abstract: Water intake is influenced by both eating and circadian rhythms, and the available literature is mixed regarding which variable exerts greater control. Previous reports primarily focused on short term manipulations, however, one study using long term light phase food restriction found that water intake patterns primarily retained circadian characteristics in male rats. To further characterize this behavioral effect, water intake and lick microstructure was analyzed in male and female rats with food access restricted to the light phase. In addition, food and water intake and lick microstructure were analyzed when water access was restricted to the light phase. In support of the previous short term, but not long term, food manipulation studies, when food access was restricted to the light phase most water intake shifted to this time frame. This shift was medicated by increased lick burst number, suggesting altered satiety signaling underling this intake pattern. When water access was restricted to the light phase, food intake was equally distributed across the light and dark phases. There was no effect of sex on the patterns of intake during any test condition. These results further our understanding of the mechanisms underlying food and water-associated and circadian intake patterns by suggesting that altered satiety signaling underlies changes in water intake. Furthermore, these results show that the timing of food access has a greater effect on water intake patterns across the light-dark cycle than water access has on food intake patterns.

papers.title: Nutrient-responsive midgut turnover is spatially controlled by serotonin signaling
papers.abstract: Barrier epithelia undergo rapid turnover, yet how spatial tissue heterogeneity and environmental cues shape turnover rates remains poorly understood. Here, we show that serotonin signaling spatially regulates homeostatic turnover of the Drosophila midgut epithelium in a nutrient-responsive manner. Organ-wide analysis revealed regions of constitutively high and low turnover, as well as areas whose renewal depends on nutrient intake. In rapidly renewing posterior regions, serotonin accumulates in enterocytes undergoing programmed cell death (erebosis) in response to nutrient availability. Serotonin signals through the conserved 5HT7 receptor to promote enteroblast (EB) maturation and migration-associated morphological changes. 5HT7 signaling is both necessary and sufficient for renewal in high-turnover regions, and its sustained disruption leads to epithelial multilayering. Mechanistically, 5HT7 signaling regulates genes involved in metabolic pathways, such as the serine biosynthesis pathway, and in the actin cytoskeleton, which drive EB maturation and morphological change, respectively. Together, our findings establish a signaling mechanism that links nutritional cues to the spatial regulation of barrier epithelium turnover.

papers.title: A transient pulse of neuronal ATF4 installs a durable non-autonomous programme promoting healthy ageing
papers.abstract: Stresses occurring transiently and early in life can have long-standing consequences for health, even long after the stress has resolved. Many environmental stressors converge on activating the integrated stress response (ISR), whose major effector is ATF4. However, it remains unknown whether transient ATF4-ISR activation early in life is a mediator of life and healthspan. Here we used inducible, reversible ATF4 gain-of-function in Drosophila to determine how the timing, duration and tissue of ATF4 activation determine ageing outcomes. We found that ATF4 induction confined to early adulthood extended healthspan, reducing mortality risk by approximately 50% across all ages and improving neuromuscular function in aged flies. Multi-organ transcriptomics showed that the acute ATF4 transcriptional response was transient, as expected, but replaced by a distinct, secondary transcriptional programme of metabolic remodelling that was associated with decreased total body protein content. By using tissue-specific ATF4 induction, we found that transient ATF4 activation in neurons was sufficient to extend lifespan, slow age-related locomotor decline and increase starvation resistance in old age. This neuron-restricted activation prevented the costs to body weight and fecundity induced by ubiquitous ATF4 activation. Transient neuronal ATF4 left a lasting non-autonomous imprint on the fat body at old age: induction of heterochromatin genes, reduced transposable element expression, and increased mitochondrial respiratory capacity. These findings show that the duration and tissue of ISR-ATF4 activation are the key determinants of ATF4 actions that promote healthy ageing, while revealing a brain-to-fat body axis initiated by neuronal ATF4 that results in lasting systemic adaptation.

papers.title: Site-, strain- and mutation-specific osteopetrosis phenotypes in mice with Clcn7 variants
papers.abstract: Background: Autosomal dominant osteopetrosis type II (ADOII) is a rare bone disorder caused primarily by heterozygous mutations in CLCN7 and characterized by increased bone mass yet fragility and marked phenotypic heterogeneity among affected individuals. The biological factors underlying this variability remain poorly understood. We investigated the effects of age, sex, genetic background, and mutation type on bone phenotypes in murine models of ADOII carrying heterozygous Clcn7 F318L/+ or G213R/+ mutations. Methods: Bone microarchitecture was assessed by micro-computed tomography in vertebrae and femora from female and male mice across multiple ages (12, 24, and 52 weeks) and strain backgrounds (FVB/NJ, C57BL/6, and 129). Vertebral biomechanical properties were estimated by micro-finite element analysis, while femoral mechanical properties were measured using three-point bending. Results: Clcn7 F318L/+ mice exhibited significantly increased trabecular bone compared with wild-type littermates at vertebral and femoral sites across the lifespan in both sexes. The magnitude of the vertebral trabecular phenotype increased with age, whereas age-related effects in the femur were more modest and site dependent. Vertebral micro-finite element analysis predicted greater stiffness and ultimate force in F318L/+ mice irrespective of age. Cortical thickness was modestly increased, particularly in female mice, but femoral mechanical properties were largely unchanged. The relative increase in vertebral trabecular bone was similar on the FVB/NJ and C57BL/6 backgrounds in males but greater on C57BL/6 in females, whereas the femoral trabecular and cortical responses were markedly attenuated on C57BL/6 in both sexes. In G213R/+ mice, the relative trabecular phenotype was similar on the C57BL/6 and 129 backgrounds, except for a greater vertebral phenotype in 129 males. Likewise, comparison of F318L/+ and G213R/+ mice demonstrated comparable vertebral phenotypes, although mutation-specific differences emerged at the femur, particularly in males. Conclusion: Collectively, these findings demonstrate that heterozygous Clcn7 mutations produce a robust osteopetrotic phenotype characterized primarily by increased trabecular bone mass that is present regardless of sex, age, genetic background, and mutation type. Age and genetic background modify its magnitude in a site- and sex-specific manner, suggesting that local factors may contribute more strongly to phenotypic variation than the specific disease-causing Clcn7 mutation. These results provide insight into determinants of phenotypic heterogeneity in ADOII and establish a framework for future mechanistic studies of osteopetrotic bone quality and fragility.

papers.title: RyR2-Mediated Ca2+ Leak Drives Progressive Arrhythmogenic Cardiomyopathy
papers.abstract: Background Abnormal sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca2+ release through ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2) is a well-established mechanism of ventricular arrhythmias. Whether persistent RyR2 dysfunction can also initiate the structural remodeling characteristic of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM) remains unknown. We tested the hypothesis that chronic RyR2-mediated Ca2+ leak is sufficient to couple electrical instability to progressive cardiomyopathy. Methods We generated a rabbit carrying the severe gain-of-function RyR2-V2475F mutation and characterized disease progression using longitudinal cardiac phenotyping, continuous electrocardiographic monitoring, cellular electrophysiology and Ca2+ imaging, histopathology, biochemical analyses, and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq). Therapeutic potential was evaluated by continuous treatment with the selective RyR2 inhibitor ent-verticilide for two months. Results RyR2-V2475F rabbits developed spontaneous ventricular tachyarrhythmias, sudden cardiac death, and progressive right ventricular (RV)-dominant fibrofatty cardiomyopathy recapitulating major features of human ACM. Malignant ventricular arrhythmias preceded overt structural remodeling and were associated at the cellular level with early spontaneous Ca2+ release and early afterdepolarizations. Early disease was characterized by remodeling of excitation-contraction coupling with preserved SR Ca2+ load and contractile function despite RyR2 dysfunction; upon disease progression, these compensatory changes were accompanied by SR Ca2+ depletion, impaired RV contractility and reduced left ventricular filling. Single-nucleus transcriptomics identified early fibroblast expansion and predicted cardiomyocyte-centered paracrine signaling before advanced fibrofatty infiltration. Cardiomyocytes also exhibited an altered lipid-metabolic transcriptome and intracellular lipid accumulation, accompanied by enhanced mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake. Selective RyR2 inhibition markedly reduced ventricular tachycardia burden and preserved RV contraction and LV filling during disease progression. Conclusions Severe RyR2 gain-of-function can lead to both malignant ventricular arrhythmias and progressive arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy in a large-animal model, establishing persistent intracellular Ca2+ dysregulation as a mechanistic link between electrical and structural heart disease. The ability of selective RyR2 inhibition to suppress arrhythmias and preserve cardiac function identifies RyR2 as a potentially actionable therapeutic target in arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.

papers.title: Locus Coeruleus activity correlates with transient elevations in breathing during opioid-induced respiratory depression
papers.abstract: A history of use remains a key risk factor for opioid-related overdose deaths in the ongoing opioid epidemic. The locus coeruleus (LC) is the principal source of noradrenergic tone and a site for opioid neuromodulation and tolerance. How a history of opioid use affects LC activity and shapes opioid-induced respiratory depression (OIRD) remains poorly understood. Using plethysmography and fiber photometry, we assessed how fentanyl affects LC activity and OIRD before and after five days of repeat opioid use (ROU). Fentanyl increased the frequency of LC bursts independent of exposure history and was coupled to transient elevations in breathing. LC coupled ventilation (LC-Ve) persisted through ROU. After ROU, OIRD magnitude diverged across mice. Mice developing an adaptive ventilatory response (AVR) showed a smaller OIRD that coincided with improved ventilation outside LC bursts and reduced LC-Ve gain. Mice with the non-adaptive response (NVR) show no improvement in OIRD or ventilation outside LC bursts, resulting in an unchanged reliance on LC-Ve. While LC-Ve reflexively counters OIRD acutely, it may also drive oscillations to destabilize blood gas homeostasis, perpetuating pathophysiology with repeat use. Thus, LC-coupled breathing appears to be a physiological signature of divergent respiratory responses with a history of fentanyl exposure.

papers.title: Partial agonists and heteromeric Kainate receptor desensitization
papers.abstract: Kainate receptors (KARs) are glutamate-gated ion channels that mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission in the central nervous system. KARs assemble as homo- or heterotetramers composed of five subunits (GluK1-5), with heteromeric assemblies representing the predominant native population. Although KARs share overall structures and basic functional properties with other ionotropic glutamate receptor subfamilies, they exhibit distinct gating kinetics, particularly with respect to desensitization. While earlier studies have demonstrated how agonist binding drives gate opening and subsequent desensitization, the mechanisms governing partial agonism and desensitization of KARs, especially in heteromeric KARs, remain incompletely understood. Here, we combine electrophysiology and microscale thermophoresis binding assays to elucidate how distinct KAR partial agonists control KAR desensitization and its recovery. While the onset rates of desensitization of homo- and heteromeric receptors activated by high/saturating concentrations of partial agonists are conserved between GluK2 and GluK2/GluK5 receptors, recovery from desensitization in heteromers is significantly slower than in homomers. Together with structural modeling and analysis of the GluK2 and GluK5 ligand binding domains (LBDs) in complex with orthosteric ligands, we show that agonist residence time and the extent of LBD bi-lobe closure across various agonists take precedence over subunit composition in governing KAR desensitization.

papers.title: Latent Transforming Growth Factor Binding Protein ? 2 promotes microfibrillar TGF-? bioavailability to drive pathologic fibrosis in remote regions of infarcted hearts
papers.abstract: Myocardial infarction (MI) initiates ventricular remodeling that extends beyond the infarct into remote, viable myocardium, where diffuse extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling and stiffening contribute to progressive dysfunction and heart failure. Latent transforming growth factor binding protein 2 (LTBP2) is an injury-induced, microfibril-associated ECM glycoprotein that, among the LTBP family, does not covalently bind latent TGF-{beta}. We asked whether LTBP2 regulates remote remodeling after MI, and how a protein lacking latent TGF-{beta}-binding capacity could influence TGF-{beta}-dependent fibrosis. Wild-type and Ltbp2-null mice underwent permanent coronary ligation or sham surgery and were followed for 28 days by echocardiography and speckle-tracking strain analysis. Remote myocardium was assessed by histology, atomic force microscopy, and quantitative proteomics. Mechanism was interrogated in primary cardiac fibroblasts using a TGF-{beta} reporter assay. Sufficiency was tested with a fibrillin-1?binding module of LTBP2 delivered as purified protein or by lentiviral expression. LTBP2 was induced in injury-activated cardiac fibroblasts and localized to infarct and remote myocardium by 7 days post-MI. Ltbp2 deletion improved 28-day survival (P=0.0272) where Ltbp2-null hearts showed preserved ejection fraction and faster diastolic strain rates, with protection concentrated in segments remote from the infarct. Remote myocardium contained less interstitial collagen and was significantly less stiff. Proteomic profiling showed enrichment of ECM organization and TGF-{beta}-responsive programs in wild-type hearts that was attenuated in knockouts. In fibroblasts, loss of LTBP2 increased LTBP1 matrix incorporation and shifted TGF-{beta} from the soluble to the matrix-bound compartment; conversely, the minimal LTBP2 module bound fibrillin-1 directly and mobilized latent TGF-{beta} from established matrix within 20 minutes. LTBP2 drives maladaptive remodeling of remote myocardium after MI by limiting matrix sequestration of latent TGF-{beta} and expanding the activatable pool, resolving how an LTBP that does not bind latent TGF-{beta} amplifies TGF-{beta}- dependent fibrosis. LTBP2 and its fibrillin-1 interaction surface may be tractable targets.

papers.title: Circadian feeding rhythm loss drives sex-specific β-cell dysfunction in diet-induced obesity
papers.abstract: Diet-induced obesity (DIO), modeled by a high-fat diet (HFD), adversely affects circadian glucose homeostasis partly by dysregulating fasting/feeding cycles. However, its impact on circadian {beta}-cell function and relevant transcriptional programs remains unclear. To investigate this, we exposed male and female C57BL/6 mice to either chow or HFD for eight weeks and assessed behavioral (feeding/activity), physiological (glucose tolerance/insulin secretion), transcriptomic (RNA sequencing (RNA-seq)), and epigenomic (Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin using Sequencing (ATAC-seq)) circadian rhythms. Additionally, we tested whether normalizing fasting/feeding cycles via time-restricted feeding (tRF) during the dark- or light-phase of the circadian cycle could mitigate DIO's deleterious effects. DIO disrupted circadian fasting/feeding rhythms, with greater disruption in males than females (p<0.05 vs. CHOW). In males, DIO abolished circadian regulation of glucose tolerance and in vivo glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) (p<0.05 vs. chow), whereas female mice maintained circadian glucose homeostasis. RNA-seq analysis of male islets revealed a 42.1% reduction in circadian-regulated transcripts under DIO, with weakened rhythms in key {beta}-cell pathways such as insulin secretion. Moreover, ATAC-Seq analysis indicated reduced chromatin accessibility of genes/pathways related to insulin secretion and glucose hemostasis under DIO (p<0.05 vs. chow) during both dark- or light-phase of the circadian cycle. Notably, dark-phase time-restricted feeding (tRF) restored circadian glucose tolerance, GSIS, and islet gene expression, whereas light-phase tRF enhanced {beta}-cell function during the normally inactive/light phase of the circadian cycle, further suppressing circadian rhythmicity of the islet transcriptome. Motif analysis indicated that DIO suppressed the activity of D-box transcription factors (TFs) (DBP and TEF) while enhancing the activity of ETS family TFs (ELK1, ETS2, ELF2, and GABPA), which was partly mitigated by dark-phase tRF. Our study demonstrates that DIO disrupts circadian {beta}-cell function and gene expression by dysregulating fasting/feeding cycles in male mice and reveals significant sex differences in how DIO affects circadian glucose homeostasis and {beta}-cell function.

papers.title: Age-related biological dysregulation quantified using metabolomics is composed of distinct subsystems with synergistic associations to health outcomes: An analysis of the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging
papers.abstract: Resilience is a fundamental component of healthy aging, whereby an organism can efficiently respond to external stressors and return to a resting biological and physiological state, known as homeostasis. This capacity declines with age in a heterogenous manner and is aggravated by biological dysregulation, a detrimental state broadly associated with health risk factors and poor outcomes. However, the underlying structure of dysregulation remains unclear, particularly in the context of older adult health trajectories. Here, we take a novel systems-based approach to the quantification of dysregulation using metabolomic data from n=9,992 older adults enrolled in the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging. We show that dysregulation across different biological systems is heritable, and exhibit distinct associations with health risk factors, indicators and outcomes, and DNA methylation patterns. Importantly, the effect of systems-specific dysregulation is cumulative, resulting in a significantly higher risk of disease incidence and death in older adults. Our findings broaden our understanding of biological dysregulation as a health state and demonstrate the value of system-specific dysregulation for effective strategies in personalized medicine and risk stratification.

papers.title: SCN- induces prestin contraction through reduced intermonomer angles and a modified transporter like movement of each monomer.
papers.abstract: Prestin is the membrane based molecular motor responsible for outer hair cell electromotility that expands and contracts in response to transmembrane voltage. How voltage brings these about is unknown but cryoEM structures in the presence of ligands has led to the extrapolation of structures with the transporter cycle and its expansion contraction coupling. We find prestin to adopt novel increasingly contracted states that are brought about by a reduced intermonomer angles in the obligate dimers and a transmembrane contraction of each monomer at its cytoplasmic half in the presence of SCN-. These changes are associated with a loss in the intermonomer beta sheet at its N terminus. There is a hyperpolarizing shift in Vh along with increased affinity for SCN-. SCN- binding at the internal binding site likely cause the structural changes since they are reversed by SCN- displacement by salicylate.

papers.title: An LRH-1 agonist reverses hepatic metabolic dysfunction in obesity
papers.abstract: Liver receptor homolog-1 (LRH-1; NR5A2) is a nuclear receptor that controls metabolic gene programs important for liver health. Here, we address two challenges with dissecting ligand-driven LRH-1 metabolism in vivo. First, we generate ME610, a potent LRH-1 agonist with favorable pharmacokinetic properties. Second, we engineer Nr5a2humLBD mice, edited to recapitulate the ligand response of the human receptor. ME610 dose-dependently induces LRH-1 target genes and reduces triglycerides in livers of Nr5a2humLBD mice. In a mouse model of diet-induced obesity (DIO), ME610 dramatically improves insulin sensitivity and reduces liver fat. Multi-omics integration of transcriptomics, lipidomics, and metabolomics data demonstrates a coordinated reversal of DIO-induced hepatic metabolic stress via changes in lipid, amino acid, and energy metabolism, with peroxisomal lipid metabolism emerging as a central process correlated to efficacy. These studies uncover new pathways through which LRH-1 regulates metabolism and demonstrate the therapeutic potential of synthetic LRH-1 agonists in obesity-associated metabolic diseases.

papers.title: Female biases in islet cell gene expression, alpha cell number, and glucagon are present early in postnatal life
papers.abstract: Biological sex significantly affects glucose homeostasis. Sex differences in insulin sensitivity in peripheral tissues play a role in this difference; however, a growing body of evidence suggests sex differences in islet cells also contribute to differential glucose homeostasis. Studies in rodent and human models have identified sex differences in alpha- and beta-cell gene expression, in islet cell composition, metabolism, and stress responses, and in circulating levels of glucoregulatory hormones. However, most of these studies used adult humans or mice, leaving the age at which these differences emerge less clear. We performed a detailed characterization of glucose homeostasis and islet biology in young male and female mice from two mouse strains widely used in diabetes research to model both Type 1 (non-obese diabetic, NOD) and Type 2 diabetes (C57BL/6J). We uncovered male-female differences in islet cell gene expression and composition, and in circulating levels of glucagon. Importantly, these differences were reproducible across both models and were present prior to diabetes-like phenotypes. Together, our data suggest sex differences in aspects of islet biology begin early in postnatal life.

papers.title: Species-Dependent Limitations of Murine Myocardium for Investigating the Combined Inotropic Effects of SERCA2a Stimulation and Myofilament Ca2+ Sensitization
papers.abstract: Impaired sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ handling and myofilament function both contribute to contractile dysfunction in heart failure. A previous study in failing human myocardium showed that combining the SERCA2a activator istaroxime (ISTA) with the Ca2+ sensitizer levosimendan (LEVO) produces greater positive inotropy than either drug alone. However, human multicellular preparations did not allow comprehensive investigation of the underlying cellular mechanisms. We therefore assessed contractile performance and Ca2+ dynamics in murine multicellular myocardial preparations and ventricular cardiomyocytes treated with ISTA (20 M), LEVO (0.5 M), or their combination. ISTA improved developed force, contraction-relaxation kinetics, and mechanical restitution. These effects were associated with increased Ca2+ transient amplitude, accelerated Ca2+ rise and decay, and enhanced sarcoplasmic reticulum reloading. Adding LEVO produced no further mechanical benefit and only minor changes in Ca2+ handling. LEVO alone elicited heterogeneous contractile responses and increased myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity in only a minority of cardiomyocytes, while consistently accelerating Ca2+ transient decay. This effect was reproduced by the phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor cilostamide, after which LEVO caused no significant additional change, consistent with a contribution of downstream cAMP-PKA signaling to the acceleration of Ca2+ removal. Thus, limited murine responsiveness to LEVO-mediated myofilament sensitization prevented mechanistic reconstruction of the additive inotropic effect observed in human myocardium, highlighting a species-dependent limitation of the mouse model for studying this combined therapy.

papers.title: No Effect of Exercise Timing on Daily Glycaemia Despite Shifts in Acute Glucose Dynamics in Participants with Normal Glucose Tolerance: A Randomised Crossover Trial
papers.abstract: Exercise is a well-established modulator of glucose regulation, but whether the time of day it is performed matters for healthy, free-living adults remains unresolved. In a randomised crossover trial, 29 healthy adults completed a single 30-minute bout of moderate-intensity exercise in the morning (07:00-10:00) and in the evening (16:00-19:00), with continuous glucose monitoring and wrist-worn activity tracking used to capture responses over an 8-day free-living protocol. Evening exercise produced a significantly greater acute reduction in blood glucose (P < 0.001) compared to morning exercise, but this did not translate into consistent differences in overall daily mean glycaemic exposure, whether measured over the calendar day or over a window aligned with exercise onset. Evening exercise was linked to greater within-day glycaemic variability than morning exercise, with the clearest evidence coming from the circadian-aligned analysis (day x timing interaction, SD: P = 0.00939; CV: P = 0.00766). Appetite rose after exercise in both conditions, with no difference by time of day. Taken together, these results show that exercise timing does not change how much glucose exposure a healthy adult accumulates over a day, but it does change the shape of the glucose response around the exercise bout itself, a distinction only visible when glucose is examined at a finer temporal resolution than daily averages allow.
